extracted.intended_audience: scientists, Royal Society members, and historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying standards for good natural-philosophical / scientific work as articulated in an 18th-century Royal Society volume; focuses on what makes modern (post‑ancient) science superior in method and evidence. Suitable for assessing historical scientific claims, methodology, and reporting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligibility of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: “No principles of nature are there allowed, but what are in themselves intelligible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories and principles accepted in inquiry should be clear and intelligible in themselves; avoid accepting opaque or ad hoc axioms. Prefer explanations whose foundational assumptions can be understood and examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mathematical reasoning as proof
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mathematical reasonings are constantly urged as valid ways of proof, in all physical inquiries where they can be brought in.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applicable, frame physical problems so they can be analysed quantitatively; deploy mathematical argument and calculation as central evidence (examples cited include roots of equations, gunnery problems, and tidal theories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical experiment and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated emphasis on experiments, dissections, observations, and the improved knowledge gained thereby (e.g., discoveries in anatomy, circulation of the blood by Harvey, microscopic observations by Leuwenhoeck).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give primacy to experimental demonstration and careful observation. Use dissection, controlled experiments, and repeated observation to establish facts; present observations as primary evidence supporting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical, systematic natural history and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for methodical compilations (e.g., 'Mr. Ray's [methodical] history of all the plants yet known') and for comprehensive descriptions and figures of plants, minerals, animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce systematic, ordered descriptions and classifications (with figures where appropriate). Detailed catalogs, indices, and consistent descriptive methods increase the value and reliability of natural-history work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental improvement and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent reference to instrument-enabled advances (telescopes, microscopes, barometers, tide‑tables, ephemerides) and that many modern discoveries depend on better instruments and measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ and report instrument-based measurements (specify instruments, methods, and calibration where possible). Innovations in instruments and measurement techniques are grounds for improved confidence in results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary support for medical and biological theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that modern medical theories are more valuable because botany, chemistry, and anatomy have been enlarged and inform practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate advances from related fields (chemistry, botany, anatomy) when developing medical or biological explanations. Cross-disciplinary evidence strengthens theoretical and practical claims in medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for modern knowledge when supported by better methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated claim that modern works (on anatomy, optics, astronomy, etc.) surpass ancient writings because of better methods, instruments, and wider learning (printing, accumulation of observations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, give weight to approaches that use improved methods, broader data, and better instrumentation; prefer up-to-date syntheses that draw on cumulative empirical work over untested ancient authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording and publication of reproducible observations and measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: The text’s many cited examples (eclipse observations, tide tables, barometer heights, ephemerides, lists of baptisms/burials, rainfall quantities) imply the value of recording exact observational data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish detailed observational records (dates, times, locations, instrument readings). Such records allow verification, comparison, and reuse (e.g., eclipses, tides, meteorological logs).
